title: The Accra Bedroom Where Herman Chinery-Hesse Wrote Software on the Bed
dek: Back in Ghana with no money for a factory, a young engineer decided his old PC was one, and showed Nestlé his bedroom only when the job was nearly done.

story.event: Starting a business software company in his parents' Accra bedroom
story.summary: In 1991 Herman Chinery-Hesse, back in Ghana after studying in Texas and working in Britain, started a software company in his bedroom at his parents' house in Accra, having no capital for the factory he had planned and no loan. Early income came from a package sold to a Ghanaian travel firm, and he did not show Nestlé the bedroom premises until its project was nearly done. Without business loans the company, later theSOFTtribe, had more than 70 staff and over 250 clients by 2005.
paragraphs: In 1991, in a bedroom of his parents' house in Accra, Herman Chinery-Hesse sat on his bed and wrote software. The room held the bed, one chair and an Amstrad XT computer with a 20-megabyte hard drive. The chair went to his partner, a former classmate who, Chinery-Hesse joked later, was so large he needed it. WIPO Magazine would later describe the Ghanaian software industry of the time as non-existent.

He had come home in 1990, after high school and university in Texas and several years in Britain, where he worked as a manufacturing engineer and wrote software freelance. His plan had been to set up a factory in Ghana. He had no money for one and could not get a loan. Looking at his PC, he said, he realised that "my computer was a factory that required no capital, only brainpower." He had a few savings, his old machine and sceptical friends who did not share his faith in Ghana as a place to start a business.

The first money came from a package he had written in Britain. He told WIPO Magazine in 2005 that he sold it to a Ghanaian travel firm before he had even reached Accra, and that the fee bought a second computer for him and his founding partner, Kojo Gyakye; in a later interview he recalled an early $5,000 job digitising a chicken farm's inventory. The firm, then called S.O.F.T., took on network software before it owned a network. When Nestlé hired it to write production management software, he did not show the visiting executives the premises, a couple of desks in his bedroom, until the work was nearly finished. "But by then it was safe to show them," he said.

The bedroom filled. When his father returned to Ghana and found people spilling out of it, Chinery-Hesse said, he moved them out to the outbuildings, where an air conditioner from the 1960s ran for five years. By 2005, renamed theSOFTtribe, the company had more than 70 staff and over 250 clients, including Unilever and Total, built without business loans. Chinery-Hesse died in September 2024, aged 61.

quote.text: he can discern what things are to be laid open, and what to be secreted, and what to be showed at half lights, and to whom and when (which indeed are arts of state, and arts of life, as Tacitus well calleth them)
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Chinery-Hesse told the Nestlé story as a joke on himself: the visitors saw the bedroom only once the work had won their confidence. Bacon counts knowing what to show, and when, among the arts of life, yet in the same breath calls a habit of hiding a poorness. Where that line lay for a two-desk firm is left open.

reflection: Most new work looks smaller up close than it does on paper. Chinery-Hesse let Nestlé see the software before they saw the bedroom, and by his account the order mattered: the executives were bemused rather than alarmed because the job was already nearly done.

You may have something you would rather people saw at half light for now: a small team, an unfinished process, an office that is really a corner of a room. That can be sensible. It helps to know, privately, what you would say if someone asked to see it today, and to be sure it is an answer you could give without flinching.
invitation: Picture someone you hope to work with walking into the place where your work really happens. Write down the one thing you would want finished before they did.

sources.supports: Born in Ireland, educated in the US and having worked in the UK, he moved to Ghana in 1990; started SOFTtribe from a bedroom in his parents' Accra house before moving to the garage; over 250 clients including Guinness, Nestlé, Unilever and the Ford Foundation.

sources.title: Tech pioneer Herman Chinery-Hesse passes away
sources.supports: Died after a cardiac arrest on a Monday evening; born in Dublin in 1963; founded the SOFTtribe in 1991; educated at Mfantsipim, Westlake High School in Austin and Texas State University.

sources.title: Herman Kojo Chinery-Hesse, Ghana's tech pioneer and founder of theSOFTtribe, passes away at 61
sources.supports: Died on 16 September 2024 after a cardiac arrest, aged 61; born in 1963 in Dublin; degree in industrial technology from Texas State University.

sources.title: Herman Kojo Chinery-Hesse: An appreciation
sources.supports: He died in mid-September 2024; quotes a 2008 profile saying that founding a software company in Ghana in 1991 was a revolutionary act and that at its height in 2003 SOFTtribe employed 80 people and booked over $1 million a year.

cross_checks.claim: He returned to Ghana around 1990 after study in the United States and work in Britain.
The company started in a bedroom in his parents' house in Accra.
He started with almost no capital and without loans.
His first software was sold to the travel industry.
Nestlé was an early client and the company grew to more than 250 clients.

research_notes: First contract: WIPO Magazine (2005) says his first contract was with a Ghanaian travel firm, landed en route to Accra with a package written while freelancing in the UK; Daily Maverick (2011) says the first programs were for the travel industry; Moguldom (2013) has him obtaining a $5,000 contract to digitise a chicken farm's inventory. The story gives the travel firm as first, per WIPO and Daily Maverick, and mentions the chicken farm as an early job he recalled later. Work in Britain: WIPO calls him a software developer in London; Daily Maverick says he worked as a manufacturing engineer; the story says he was a manufacturing engineer who also wrote software freelance, which reconciles both. Partner: WIPO names his founding partner as Kojo Gyakye; Daily Maverick mentions an unnamed former classmate who needed the chair; the story assumes these are the same person only so far as both are called his partner and does not merge the details beyond that. Premises: Daily Maverick says his father moved them to the outbuildings; HumanIPO says the garage; the story uses Daily Maverick's account in his words. Staff figures: WIPO (2005) gives over 70 staff and over 250 clients; a 2008 profile quoted by the Ghanaian Times gives 80 employees and over $1 million revenue at the 2003 peak; the story uses WIPO's dated 2005 figures. Year of return: 1990 (HumanIPO, Moguldom; WIPO's 'fifteen years ago' in 2005); founding 1991 (Graphic, Citi Newsroom). Funding: bootstrapped; WIPO says growth came without business loan financing until an international investment group took a stake around 2005. WIPO spells his first name 'Hermann' and once 'Chinnery-Hesse'; Ghanaian outlets use Herman Chinery-Hesse. The Inc. (2008) profile cited by others is blocked (403) and is not cited directly. The Bacon passage is about the arts of policy in public life; it is applied by analogy to a small firm's choice about what to show a client.
